Dataset title: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)
Description: The Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA) collects data for new residential construction. The SOMA reports provide information on amenities, rent/sales price levels, number of units, type of building, and the number of units taken off the market (absorbed). The data are collected at quarterly intervals until 12 months expire or until the units in a building are completely absorbed, which may occur sooner.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:

Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>

Policy: <level>

Section was enacted as part of the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1970, and not as part of the National Housing Act which comprises this chapter.

12 U.S. Code § 1701z-2 - Advanced technologies, methods, and materials for housing construction, rehabilitation, and maintenance

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes

prev | next
(a) General acceptance; costs, reduction; health and safety restrictions on expanded housing production

The Secretary shall require, to the greatest extent feasible, the employment of new and improved technologies, methods, and materials in housing construction, rehabilitation, and maintenance under programs administered by him with a view to reducing costs, and shall encourage and promote the acceptance and application of such advanced technology, methods, and materials by all segments of the housing industry, communities, industries engaged in urban development activities, and the general public. To the extent feasible, in connection with the construction, major rehabilitation, or maintenance of any housing assisted under section 1701z–1 of this title, the Secretary shall assure that there is no restraint by contract, building code, zoning ordinance, or practice against the employment of new or improved technologies, techniques, materials, and methods or of preassembled products which may reduce the cost or improve the quality of such construction, rehabilitation, and maintenance, and therefore stimulate expanded production of housing, except where such restraint is necessary to insure safe and healthful working and living conditions.

(b) Experimental construction under approved housing plans on Federal or other lands with view toward ultimate mass housing production; use of section 1701z–1 funds and authority

To encourage large-scale experimentation in the use of new technologies, methods, and materials, with a view toward the ultimate mass production of housing and related facilities, the Secretary shall wherever feasible conduct programs under section 1701z–1 of this title in which qualified organizations, public and private, will submit plans for development and production of housing and related facilities using such new advances on Federal land which has been made available or acquired by the Secretary for the purpose of this subsection or on other land where (1) local building regulations permit such experimental construction, or (2) necessary variances from building regulations can be granted. The Secretary may utilize the funds and authority available to him under the provisions of section 1701z–1 of this title to assist in the implementation of plans which he approves.

(c) Acquisition, use, and disposal of property; transfer of excess property

Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Secretary is authorized, in connection with projects under this title [12 U.S.C. 1701z–1 et seq.], to acquire, use and dispose of any land and other property required for the project as he deems necessary. Notwithstanding the provisions of chapters 1 to 11 of title 40 and division C (except sections 3302, 3307(e), 3501(b), 3509, 3906, 4710, and 4711) of subtitle I of title 41, any land which is excess property within the meaning of chapters 1 to 11 of title 40 and division C (except sections 3302, 3307(e), 3501(b), 3509, 3906, 4710, and 4711) of subtitle I of title 41 and which is determined by the Secretary to be suitable in furtherance of the purposes of subsection (b) may be transferred to the Secretary upon his request.

(d) Technical assistance; reports; general dissemination and form of reports, data, and information

In order to effectively carry out his activities under section 1701z–1 of this title, the Secretary is authorized to provide such advice and technical assistance as may be required and to pay for the cost of writing and publishing reports on activities and undertakings financed under section 1701z–1 of this title, as well as reports on similar activities and undertakings, not so financed, which are of significant value in furthering the purposes of that section. He may disseminate (without regard to the provisions of section 3204 of title 39 or section 4154 of such title with respect to any period before the effective date of such section 3204 as provided in section 15(a) of the Postal Reorganization Act) any reports, data, or information acquired or held under this title [12 U.S.C. 1701z–1 et seq.], including related data and information otherwise available to the Secretary through the operation of the programs and activities of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, in such form as he determines to be most useful to departments, establishments, and agencies of Federal, State, and local governments, to industry, and to the general public.

(e) Contracts or grants; authority; advance and progress payments; work limitation

The Secretary is authorized to carry out the functions authorized in section 1701z–1 of this title either directly or, without regard to section 6101 of title 41, by contract or by grant. Advance and progress payments may be made under such contracts or grants without regard to the provisions of subsections (a) and (b) of section 3324 of title 31 and such contracts or grants may be made for work to continue for not more than four years from the date thereof.

(f) Utilization of facilities of other agencies; working agreements, cooperative agreements, contract authority, receipt of funds, and exercise of section 1701c(c) powers

In carrying out activities under section 1701z–1 of this title, the Secretary shall utilize to the fullest extent feasible the available facilities of other Federal departments and agencies, and shall consult with, and make recommendations to, such departments and agencies. The Secretary may enter into working agreements with such departments and agencies and contract or make grants on their behalf or have such departments and agencies contract or make grants on his behalf and such departments and agencies are hereby authorized to execute such contracts and grants. The Secretary is authorized to make or accept reimbursement for the cost of such activities. The Secretary is further authorized to undertake activities under this title [12 U.S.C. 1701z–1 et seq.] under cooperative agreements with industry and labor, agencies of State or local governments, educational institutions, and other organizations. He may enter into contracts with and receive funds from such agencies, institutions, and organizations, and may exercise any of the other powers vested in him by section 1701c(c) of this title.

(g) Information and data; restriction on use or identification

The Secretary is authorized to request and receive such information or data as he deems appropriate from private individuals and organizations, and from public agencies. Any such information or data shall be used only for the purposes for which it is supplied, and no publication shall be made by the Secretary whereby the information or data furnished by any particular person or establishment can be identified, except with the consent of such person or establishment.

(Pub. L. 91–609, title V, § 502, Dec. 31, 1970, 84 Stat. 1784; Pub. L. 94–375, § 23(c), Aug. 3, 1976, 90 Stat. 1078; Pub. L. 98–479, title II, § 203(k), Oct. 17, 1984, 98 Stat. 2231.)

{"date":"2026-09-09T17:55:45","content":{"rendered":"

The Department of Housing and Urban Development proposed plans for a large-scale reorganization to accommodate a significantly downsized workforce, but then quickly withdrew those plans for unknown reasons, documents obtained by Federal News Network show.

HUD initially issued a preview of its “notice of intent to reorganize” on Sept. 4 in the Federal Register’s public inspection repository. But later in the day, HUD’s Office of General Counsel submitted a request for the document to be withdrawn from public inspection and to cancel its formal publication in the Federal Register, without providing a reason for the withdrawal.

The draft reorganization plans and withdrawal notice, both viewed by Federal News Network, show that HUD was planning to reorganize and consolidate many of the department’s components, in large part due to thousands of employee separations that occurred throughout 2025.

“Certain offices were particularly impacted by these departures, leaving them constrained in the ability to accomplish departmental goals and objectives,” HUD wrote in the now-rescinded document.

HUD is currently staffed with around 5,800 employees, compared with about 8,800 during fiscal 2024. The headcount reductions were driven by employee separations through the deferred resignation program (DRP) and other voluntary separation programs during 2025.

“Current staffing levels are almost 35% below historic staffing levels and this reorganization will provide HUD with the ability to operate even more effectively at current staffing levels, ultimately carrying forward savings from the reduced salaries and expenses of the department,” the document, signed by HUD Deputy Secretary Andrew Hughes, states.

It’s not clear why the notice was withdrawn or whether HUD plans to pursue a reorganization in the future. Federal News Network’s emails seeking details from HUD on the draft reorganization plans and the reason for rescinding the notice were not immediately answered.

According to the draft proposal, the large-scale reorganization is meant to streamline the department in response to markedly lower staffing levels. The reorganization would not relocate any employees or further reduce staffing, HUD wrote.

The document described plans to merge some smaller departmental units and move some divisions under different chains of command.

For instance, HUD’s Office of the Chief Information Officer would create a new customer experience division, while consolidating its contract and financial management arms.

The now-withdrawn plan also proposed consolidating functions of the Office of Public and Indian Housing due to staffing reductions in that component. It would put all public housing work under one office, and all voucher programs under another.

“This will streamline both processes and program administration,” HUD wrote.

The Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, the Office of Community Planning and Development, the Office of Policy Development and Research, the Office of Public Affairs, and the Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes would each undergo some level of consolidation. Ginnie Mae would be restructured and have some new branches added.

The Federal Housing Administration’s Office of Single Family Housing would transition from a “geographic-based” to a “function-based” model. And FHA’s Office of Operations would be merged with other support offices “to increase operational efficiency and eliminate redundancies,” the document states.

HUD’s Office of General Counsel would be reorganized to consolidate headquarters, regional and field offices into a single “unified structure.”

The Office of the Chief Financial Officer would be restructured into three divisions, focusing on budget assistance, financial management and travel management. And the Office of the Chief Human Capital Officer would create two new divisions: one focused on implementing “new workforce accountability and suitability measures,” and a “business partner division” that would consolidate work currently housed under individual program offices.

“The reorganization is expected to significantly enhance operational efficiency, as well as improve HUD’s program delivery and the service provided to HUD's customers,” the document states.

The draft reorganization plans come as the Trump administration is seeking to reduce overall spending at HUD. The White House’s 2027 budget proposal calls for a $73.5 billion discretionary budget for HUD, representing a $10.7 billion or 13% decrease from enacted 2026 spending levels.

HUD shared its proposed reorganization plans with Congress in April, according to the draft notice document.

“This notice reflects the next step in moving forward with these plans,” HUD wrote in the now-rescinded document.

HUD proposed starting the reorganization process 90 days after publishing the notice and projected completion of its restructuring plans during fiscal 2027. But since the notice was withdrawn, it’s not clear when or if these plans will take effect.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)
Description: The Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA) collects data for new residential construction. The SOMA reports provide information on amenities, rent/sales price levels, number of units, type of building, and the number of units taken off the market (absorbed). The data are collected at quarterly intervals until 12 months expire or until the units in a building are completely absorbed, which may occur sooner.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)

**Research checked: October 9, 2026.** This report distinguishes documented program facts from analytical and preservation recommendations. Most sources are Census Bureau, HUD, or federal information-collection records.

## Executive summary

**Your title and description are accurate, but the description needs several qualifications.** SOMA is not a survey of all new residential construction. It follows newly completed residential buildings containing **five or more housing units**, using the Census Bureau’s Survey of Construction as its sampling base. Its central measure is **initial market absorption**—how quickly newly built apartments are first rented, or condominium/cooperative apartments are first sold.

The **U.S. Census Bureau conducts and publishes SOMA for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)**. HUD’s Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R) is the sponsoring office identified in the federal information-collection records.

SOMA’s distinctive value is that it connects **new housing supply, asking prices, building/unit characteristics, and initial rental or sales outcomes**. It fills a gap between construction statistics and surveys of the existing housing stock.

For researchers and preservationists, the most important cautions are:

- **Collection occurs continuously:** new buildings enter the sample monthly, while each building is interviewed approximately 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after completion, as necessary.
- **Absorption is not ongoing occupancy or the vacancy rate of the entire housing stock.**
- **Completion quarter, absorption observation period, and publication date are different dates.**
- Public products are **weighted aggregate estimates**, not an open property-level database.
- Historical definitions, weighting, price categories, and dissemination formats have changed.
- **A Census API exists**, alongside the interactive Table Creator and historical files.
- Preserving only the Table Creator webpage would not preserve the dataset: data exports, API metadata, methodology, questionnaires, and release versions are also essential.

Sources: [Census overview](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about.html), [FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/faq.html), [developer documentation](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/soma.html).

---

## 1. Dataset identity and corrected description

| Attribute | Finding |
|---|---|
| Official current title | **Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units** |
| Acronym | SOMA |
| Alternative administrative title | **Survey of Market Absorption of New Apartment Buildings**, used in OMB records |
| Collector and principal publisher | U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce |
| Sponsor | HUD, Office of Policy Development and Research |
| Dataset type | Sample-survey program producing quarterly, annual, and prior-four-quarter aggregate estimates |
| Principal subject | Initial rental/sales absorption of newly completed multifamily housing |
| Sampling unit | Residential building with five or more units |
| Reporting unit | Primarily housing units, rather than buildings |
| Preferred respondents | Building managers or rental/sales agents; owners and builders may also respond |
| Follow-up duration | Up to 12 months after completion; interviews can stop sooner upon complete absorption |

A more precise catalog description would be:

> The Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA), conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau for HUD, measures the initial rental or sales absorption of newly completed residential buildings containing five or more housing units. Buildings are selected monthly from the Survey of Construction. An initial interview approximately three months after completion collects information on unit and building characteristics, amenities, asking rent or sales price, and initial absorption. Follow-up interviews occur at approximately six, nine, and twelve months when necessary, ending sooner if all units have been absorbed. Public products provide weighted aggregate estimates, with applicable uncertainty measures and publication restrictions.

This retains the substance of your description while clarifying the universe, timing, price concept, and statistical nature of the products. [Census overview and FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/faq.html)

## 2. Who publishes it, and why?

### Institutional responsibilities

**Census Bureau**

- Draws the SOMA sample from Survey of Construction records.
- Conducts interviews through its field organization.
- Processes and estimates the statistics.
- Publishes tables, documentation, and machine-readable access.
- Protects respondent confidentiality.

**HUD/PD&R**

- Sponsors the survey.
- Identifies its housing-policy research purpose.
- Is the agency responsible for its Paperwork Reduction Act information-collection approval.
- Uses the results to assess whether new apartment construction is meeting present and future housing needs.

The program’s stated purpose is to determine whether rental-housing supply is keeping pace with current and future needs, and to measure how different types of newly built rental and ownership units are absorbed during their first year. [2026 information-collection request](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202606-2528-001)

### Authority versus a dataset-specific mandate

SOMA rests on **broad housing-research authority**, rather than a statute that explicitly orders an indefinitely continuing survey named SOMA.

- **12 U.S.C. § 1701z-1** authorizes and directs HUD’s Secretary to undertake research, studies, testing, and demonstrations relating to HUD’s mission.
- **12 U.S.C. § 1701z-2** provides related powers, including publishing and disseminating reports and data, contracting or making grants, using other federal agencies’ facilities, and requesting information subject to restrictions on identification.
- These provisions originated in **Title V of the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1970**, Public Law 91-609.
- Census’s respondent letter identifies **13 U.S.C. §§ 8 and 9** as its authority and confidentiality basis.

The OMB records contain apparent metadata errors: they label the law “United States Housing Act of 1970” and display one citation as “170z-2.” The statutory text supports the corrected references above. [§ 1701z-1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/12/1701z-1), [§ 1701z-2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/12/1701z-2), [respondent letter](https://omb.report/icr/202404-2528-003/doc/142088601.pdf)

### OMB approval and respondent burden

- **OMB control number:** **2528-0013**.
- The 2024 approval record lists **48,000 annual responses**, **6,000 annual burden hours**, and **$0 additional respondent cost burden**.
- These are administrative burden estimates—not counts of observed housing units or unique sampled buildings.
- Historical supporting documentation describes participation as **voluntary**, with no penalties for failing to answer.
- The 2024 advance letter estimates approximately **30 minutes for initial and subsequent interviews combined**.

The 2024 approval’s listed expiration date was **September 30, 2026**. A renewal submitted July 23, 2026 requested an extension without change; the record located in this research showed it as **received in OIRA**, not a completed approval. Thus, I cannot confirm the replacement expiration date from the material retrieved.

**This is not evidence that SOMA has stopped.** Census’s release calendar continues into 2027. [2024 approval](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202404-2528-003), [2026 renewal](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202606-2528-001), [historical supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/201012-2528-003/doc/22094502.pdf)

## 3. History and important changes

| Date/period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| **1970/early 1970s** | Census describes the program as operating since the early 1970s. HUD’s historical series includes 1970 observations. Those facts establish a long series, but not an exact first interview or publication date. |
| **1990** | New weighting/ratio-estimation adjustments adopted to improve completion estimates. |
| **1992** | Further modification to weighting. Census explicitly cautions against unqualified comparison of completion counts before and after this change. |
| **2002** | Collection of senior-housing information began. |
| **April 2014** | Computer-assisted interviewing on laptops began for January 2014 completions. Asking-rent and sales-cost categories changed; utilities and amenities questions also changed. Earlier completion cohorts continued on paper during the transition. |
| **September 27, 2018** | Dissemination shifted to **SOMA Table Creator**. Traditional quarterly, annual, and characteristics reports/tables ceased being produced in their historical format; earlier releases remained available. |
| **2016 onward** | Completion years covered by Table Creator, including years preceding its launch. |
| **June 2019** | Asking-rent and asking-sale-price categories changed again, beginning with first-quarter 2019 completions. |
| **May 2024** | Table Creator interface updated with interactive selection criteria and grid. |
| **2026** | New release dates and an OMB renewal request document continued program activity. |

Sources: [Census history](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/housing/survey-of-market-absorption.html), [HUD historical series](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/periodicals/ushmc/winter12/USHMC_4q12_historical.pdf), [user notes](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/technical-documentation/user-note.html), [2014–2015 transition documentation](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2015/demo/q115report.pdf), [Table Creator history](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/table-creator.html).

**Preservation implication:** SOMA should be cataloged as a continuing statistical series with multiple product formats and methodological eras, not as one timeless file with a fixed schema.

## 4. Coverage: what is—and is not—represented?

### Basic scope

SOMA concerns **newly constructed buildings with five or more housing units**. It does not describe the whole housing market, and it does not cover one-to-four-unit construction in its SOMA universe.

Census’s Source and Accuracy page states that SOMA **does not include buildings completed in areas that do not issue building permits**. This is important because the parent Survey of Construction has broader procedures, including non-permit areas; one should not automatically transfer SOC’s entire coverage to SOMA. [Source and Accuracy](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/technical-documentation/source-accuracy.html)

### Core series versus broader characteristics tables

Historical descriptions emphasize **privately financed, nonsubsidized, unfurnished rental units** and condominium/cooperative units. Current public metadata also identifies:

- Furnished/unfurnished apartment distinctions.
- Annual subsidized/tax-credit-unit estimates.
- Services offered for age-restricted units.
- Broader building and unit characteristics.

Consequently, **“SOMA excludes every subsidized or furnished unit” is too broad a description of the whole program**. The universe of a particular table or absorption series must be checked separately.

There is also some inconsistency across Census explanatory pages. The “Characteristics of Data” page describes particular federal subsidy categories and says privately financed data include privately owned housing subsidized by state and local governments, while the glossary uses a broader subsidy definition. Preserve both sources, but use the **questionnaire and year-specific technical statement** to resolve a specific analysis. [Characteristics of Data](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/characteristics-data.html), [glossary](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/glossary.html), [API variables](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/soma/variables.html)

### Explicit exclusions and classification rules

Census identifies these as outside scope:

- Time-share units.
- Continuing-care retirement units.
- Turnkey units privately built for, and sold to, local public housing authorities after completion.

Units initially intended for condominium/cooperative sale but subsequently offered for rent by the builder or owner are counted as **rental apartments**. This classification can affect comparisons between rental and ownership construction. [Characteristics of Data](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/characteristics-data.html)

### Geography

Public access supports:

- United States totals.
- Four Census regions: Northeast, Midwest, South, and West.
- Broad **CBSA/principal-city status** classifications.

The Table Creator guide says users cannot select both region and CBSA status in the same query. The API’s geography metadata lists **U.S. and region** as geographic levels; CBSA status also appears as a table characteristic.

**CBSA status is not equivalent to a dataset of individual metropolitan areas.** Do not assume contemporary city, county, tract, state, or named-metro estimates are available. Historical materials referring to selected metropolitan-area products should not be treated as a promise about current geography. [User guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/guidance/user-guide/SOMATC_Users_Guide.pdf), [API geography metadata](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/soma/geography.json)

## 5. What does SOMA measure?

### Absorption

Census defines absorption as the initial rental or sale of a unit following construction, after which it is no longer available on the market.

For a particular completion cohort, an absorption rate at a stated horizon can be understood as:

\[
100 \times \frac{\text{estimated eligible units initially absorbed by that horizon}}
{\text{estimated eligible units completed in the cohort}}
\]

The exact denominator and eligibility restrictions should follow the selected table.

**Absorption does not measure:**

- Whether the first tenant still occupies the unit.
- Subsequent tenant turnover or resale.
- All vacant housing.
- Whether the unit is affordable to local residents.
- The experience or demographics of the people who moved in.

### Characteristics

Available topics, depending on product and year, include:

- Asking monthly rent.
- Asking sale price.
- Number of bedrooms.
- Number of units in the building.
- Number of stories.
- Amenities.
- Furnished/unfurnished status.
- Age-restricted housing and services.
- Subsidized/tax-credit categories.
- Region and CBSA status.
- Units completed and absorption measures at specified follow-up horizons.

These are **asking-price statistics**, not automatically realized transaction prices, effective rents after concessions, or household housing expenditures. Medians may be interpolated from grouped price categories; older series can have open-ended upper categories.

Sources: [glossary](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/glossary.html), [API variable inventory](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/soma/variables.html), [user guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/guidance/user-guide/SOMATC_Users_Guide.pdf).

## 6. Collection, sampling, and estimation

### Collection cycle

1. SOC identifies a newly completed eligible building.
2. The building enters SOMA’s monthly sample.
3. An interview occurs approximately **three months after completion**.
4. Follow-ups occur at **six, nine, and twelve months**, if necessary.
5. Collection ends earlier if the building’s units have been completely absorbed.

Respondents are usually building managers or rental/sales agents, rather than tenants.

An important completion definition appears in the 2024 statistical supporting statement: a multifamily building is classified as complete when **at least 50% of its units are available for occupancy**. Thus, “completion” need not mean every unit was ready on the same day. [2024 statistical supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202404-2528-003/doc/142087401.pdf)

### Sample design

SOMA inherits a multistage sample from SOC, involving:

- Primary sampling units.
- Permit-issuing places within sampled areas.
- Construction permits/buildings.

Selection of five-plus-unit permits with certainty **within sampled places** does not make SOMA a census of all U.S. multifamily buildings.

The 2024 supporting statement describes a provision to subsample when monthly completed buildings exceed 1,200, and says SOMA had not used that subsampling since 2005. Treat these as **vintage-specific design statements**, not permanent guarantees.

### Estimation and response

The same supporting statement describes:

- Base weights equal to inverse selection probabilities.
- Weighted aggregation of building counts.
- A ratio-estimation adjustment.
- A reported response rate above 90%.

That response-rate statement is not a verified response rate for every later cohort. Researchers should consult the relevant year’s source-and-accuracy document for current weighting, nonresponse treatment, editing, and variance procedures. [Statistical supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202404-2528-003/doc/142087401.pdf)

## 7. Publication schedule, revision, and interpretation

### Three dates must be kept separate

For example:

- **First-quarter 2026 completions** identify the construction cohort.
- **Second-quarter 2026 absorptions** refer to its initial follow-up period.
- **August 2026** is the scheduled publication month.

Census’s release calendar lists:

| Product | Scheduled release |
|---|---|
| Q2 2026 absorptions / Q1 2026 completions | August 2026 |
| Q3 2026 absorptions / Q2 2026 completions | November 2026 |
| Q4 2026 absorptions / Q3 2026 completions | February 2027 |
| 2025 completions annual tables | February 2027 |
| Q1 2027 absorptions / Q4 2026 completions | May 2027 |

These are **scheduled dates**, not an independent audit of whether every release occurred. [Release calendar](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/about/release-dates.html)

Quarterly data are revised in ensuing quarters. Later follow-up outcomes also become available as a cohort ages. Annual, quarterly, and prior-four-quarter products must not be mixed indiscriminately.

Census’s history page retains an older publication schedule and descriptions of former reports. For current timing, use the dedicated release calendar.

### Seasonal adjustment

The user guide describes a separate seasonally adjusted estimates spreadsheet for **unfurnished apartments**. Do not assume every displayed Table Creator value is seasonally adjusted, or apply an adjustment designed for one series to unrelated breakdowns. Preserve the adjustment file and its vintage with any analysis. [User guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/guidance/user-guide/SOMATC_Users_Guide.pdf)

## 8. Quality, uncertainty, and common analytical hazards

### Sampling and nonsampling error

SOMA is a sample survey. Estimates are subject to:

- Sampling variability.
- Coverage limitations.
- Nonresponse.
- Reporting and interview error.
- Classification, processing, and editing error.

Published margins of error reflect sampling uncertainty, **not every source of error**. Table Creator offers **90% margins of error**.

### Suppression and missing-value symbols

The Table Creator guide documents:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | Suppressed/withheld estimate |
| **X** | No sampled units meet the cell’s conditions |
| **.** | Data forthcoming |

Its listed suppression conditions include:

- Coefficient of variation **at least 30%**.
- **Five or fewer buildings** contributing to a unit estimate.
- Median-cost MOE suppression when the median lies in the upper unbounded price category.

**Never convert these symbols to zero.** “No sampled units” is not proof that no such units exist in the population. Suppression is also informative: it often indicates small samples or instability, so dropping suppressed rows can bias the apparent distribution. [User guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/guidance/user-guide/SOMATC_Users_Guide.pdf)

### Practical safeguards

- Preserve estimates **and** MOEs and override/status fields.
- Compare like completion cohorts, unit types, universes, and horizons.
- Do not average percentages across groups without appropriate denominators.
- Do not average regional medians to derive a national median.
- Account for rounding: published components may not sum exactly.
- Treat rolling four-quarter estimates as overlapping observations.
- Deflate nominal rents/prices explicitly for long-run comparisons.
- Harmonize price bands across the 2014 and 2019 changes.
- Recognize that changes in bedroom, regional, or building-size composition can move overall medians.
- Do not interpret descriptive absorption differences as causal effects of zoning, subsidies, or interest rates.

## 10. Typical users and public benefits

### Documented users

Census explicitly identifies:

- Builders.
- Banks/bankers.
- Market analysts.
- Land planners.
- Government officials.

HUD’s stated use is assessing whether new construction meets present and future needs. [Census history](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/housing/survey-of-market-absorption.html)

### How different communities can use it

| Community | Value |
|---|---|
| Developers and lenders | Benchmark initial lease-up/sales speed and assess broad market conditions. |
| Housing agencies and planners | Examine the composition and price levels of new multifamily supply. |
| Economists and data scientists | Study housing cycles and relationships among completions, asking prices, and absorption. |
| Journalists and advocates | Test broad claims about new apartments sitting unrented or new supply concentrating in expensive categories. |
| Data librarians | Support reproducible access to a long-running federal housing series. |
| Preservationists | Retain evidence of changing construction, prices, housing characteristics, and statistical practices. |

The last four rows describe reasonable applications, not a measured census of actual SOMA users.

### Benefits to the public

1. **An independent public benchmark:** users need not rely exclusively on proprietary real-estate analytics.
2. **A link between construction and market outcomes:** completion counts alone cannot show how quickly supply is taken up.
3. **Evidence on the kind of housing being produced:** bedrooms, price categories, amenities, and senior-housing characteristics.
4. **Long-run historical context:** the series spans multiple housing booms, recessions, and policy eras.
5. **More accountable debate:** transparent definitions and uncertainty measures help distinguish evidence from anecdote.

These benefits are plausible and supported by the program’s purpose; I found no evaluation quantifying SOMA’s monetary public benefit or attributing particular policy outcomes to it.

### What activists should not conclude from SOMA alone

- Slow absorption does **not** prove absence of housing need: asking prices may exceed residents’ ability to pay.
- Fast absorption does **not** prove affordability.
- National or regional outcomes do **not** settle a neighborhood-level zoning dispute.
- SOMA does not directly identify tenant race, income, displacement, evictions, or rent burden.
- It is not a substitute for an inventory of subsidized housing or an evaluation of subsidy programs.

## 11. Privacy and reuse

Census’s respondent letter promises that responses will not be publicly released in a way that identifies the respondent or business. It cites Title 13 confidentiality, the Privacy Act, and cybersecurity safeguards. HUD’s research authority also restricts identifying publication of supplied information. The public products are disclosure-reviewed aggregate statistics. Open access to these products does not authorize disclosure of confidential source records.

Federal government statistical products are generally reusable, but librarians should record the publisher’s applicable terms rather than inventing a dataset-specific Creative Commons license. Third-party material, branding, and confidential records require separate treatment.

Recommended citation elements:

> U.S. Census Bureau, for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. *Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units*. [Product/table or API selection], [completion cohort], [absorption horizon], [release/retrieval date], [URL].

### Main preservation risks

- **Interactive application dependence:** static webpage capture may not retain its data.
- **Live revisions:** a later API call can differ from an earlier one.
- **Fragmented hosting:** reports, directories, metadata, and regulatory records are in different systems.
- **Methodological breaks:** a long time series can appear continuous while definitions change.
- **Misleading filesystem dates:** many old table folders show 2016 modification dates, evidently reflecting hosting history rather than original data years.
- **Version ambiguity:** the documentation directory contains “old” and revised files; preserve their lineage rather than silently replacing them.

Use immutable raw snapshots, SHA-256 checksums, redundant storage, and a manifest connecting each data vintage to its documentation. Convert spreadsheets to durable open formats where useful, but retain originals, footnotes, formulas, and layout.

# SOMA dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**

**Bottom line:** I found **no evidence that SOMA’s historical data have been systematically removed or that the survey has been terminated**. The strongest risks are institutional: substantial staffing losses at Census and HUD, broad rather than survey-specific statutory protection, and budget/reorganization pressures. These create a credible risk of future disruption, but do not establish that published SOMA estimates are currently unreliable.

One important qualification concerns the **pending OMB renewal**: its previously listed expiration date has passed, but timely renewal submissions can legally continue while OMB reviews them. Accordingly, a printed expiration date alone is not evidence that collection has stopped.

## Scope and approach

This assessment covers the Census Bureau’s SOMA program, including its historical files, Table Creator, API, and supporting documentation. Census conducts SOMA for HUD’s Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R), so both institutions’ capacity matters.

I distinguish:

- **Observed dataset changes** from broader agency risks.
- **Proposed budgets** from enacted funding.
- **Job advertisements** from actual staffing losses.
- **Ordinary revisions and statistical suppression** from removal or manipulation.

“No Known Issue” means no qualifying problem was identified—not that every historical file or publication date has been exhaustively audited.
